answer.rationale: The shock is price-driven churn in the SMB base, so the only candidate that acts directly on the stated cause is promotional pricing; onboarding simplification and activation messaging address acquisition/activation rather than retention of already-price-sensitive accounts, referral incentives target established customers, and enterprise sales-assist is scoped to a different segment (exp_44 explicitly 'Enterprise only'). However, the evidence quality is asymmetric. The two directions I actually re-verified this cycle (exp_86 onboarding, exp_44 enterprise) both carry retention and revenue-quality readouts. memory_73, the basis for promotional pricing, is a consolidated day-31 summary with the source archived and no recoverable retention, margin, or revenue-quality figures — it reports 'acquisition and revenue lift' only. Against a primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, that is exactly the missing dimension: discounting into a competitor's second cut risks resetting the price anchor, compressing margin on renewal cohorts, and pulling in low-intent accounts whose revenue is not durable. Matching a deeper cut can also invite a third cut, which is a losing position to broad-rollout into. So I take the price-facing action but deliberately cap exposure: a small guarded test on a bounded slice of the price-sensitive SMB segment, time-boxed with an explicit expiry so it does not become the new list price, instrumented for margin-adjusted qualified revenue and 60/90-day retention rather than acquisition count alone, and with a pre-committed stop condition. When the archive reopens, memory_73 is the first verification request — its retention and margin gap is what currently limits confidence — followed by memory_31, memory_57, and memory_91, all of which are similarly unverified consolidations I am not treating as settled. If memory_73 fails verification, the fallback is the confirmed onboarding/time-to-value work as a non-price value response.
